13020: Jewish and post-Holocaust readers ask whether 'fulfilment' still implies that Judaism today is empty. Others note it can underplay the genuine discontinuity Hebrews asserts, or alternatively soften the sharpness of the warnings.
13021: Jewish-Christian intramural debate (new or renewed covenantalism)
13022: Richard Hays, Mark Nanos, Pamela Eisenbaum, and in different ways Luke Timothy Johnson.
13023: Hebrews comes from inside first-century Judaism before 'Judaism' and 'Christianity' were separate religions. Like the Qumran community, which also saw itself as the people of the new covenant, the author argues about the right way to be faithful to Israel's God, now through Messiah Jesus. Hays calls it Jewish sectarian 'new covenantalism'; Nanos prefers 'renewed covenantalism'.
13024: It matches the book's total immersion in Jewish Scripture and worship, its silence about Gentile-Jewish tension, and its historical setting in the decades before the parting of the ways.
13025: Critics say it can blur the real newness Hebrews claims for Jesus' once-for-all sacrifice, and that a sect claiming the old system is 'near vanishing' is still making exclusive claims that later readers will hear as replacement. Some note that the audience may have included many Gentiles.
13027: Older scholars such as James Moffatt and Ceslas Spicq, and with nuance Harold Attridge and James Thompson.
13028: Hebrews thinks in the categories of Alexandrian Jewish philosophy: the heavenly, true and eternal versus the earthly, copied and passing. Its affinity with Philo of Alexandria suggests an author like Apollos, an Alexandrian Jew.
13029: It explains vocabulary such as 'shadow', 'copy' and 'true tabernacle' and the polished Greek rhetoric of the book.
13030: Ronald Williamson and others showed the differences from Philo are deep: Hebrews has a decisive historical event, an end of the ages and a coming city. Shared vocabulary does not mean shared worldview.
13032: C. K. Barrett, Lincoln Hurst, David Moffitt, and many recent commentators.
13033: The two-level picture of Hebrews is Jewish apocalyptic: a heavenly temple where God is enthroned (as in 1 Enoch, Daniel and the Qumran Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice), two ages, and a coming kingdom that cannot be shaken. Melchizedek speculation like 11QMelchizedek belongs here too.
13034: It accounts for the future orientation of the book (the 'coming world', Heb 2:5; the 'city to come', Heb 13:14) and the emphasis on resurrection and ascension.
13035: Hebrews does use philosophical vocabulary, and many scholars think the either-or is false: a Hellenistic Jewish preacher could blend apocalyptic structure with Platonist language.
13038: Used about thirteen times to compare what God gave earlier with what he gives in the Son: better hope, covenant, promises, sacrifices, possession, country, resurrection. It is a comparison of good and better within one plan.
13041: To bring to completion or goal; in priestly use, to consecrate for service. Jesus was 'made perfect through sufferings' (qualified as priest), and the law could not 'perfect' worshippers, that is, bring them fully into God's presence.
13044: A broker or guarantor who stands between two parties. In a patronage society, the mediator brings clients near to a great patron. Jesus mediates a better covenant and guarantees it with his life.
13047: The Septuagint word for berit, God's binding relational commitment to a people. In 9:16-17 the author plays on its other meaning, a will that takes effect at death.
13048: Belief in doctrines, or certainty without evidence.
13049: Trust, loyalty and faithfulness toward a faithful God, shown over time in obedience and endurance. Jesus is the 'pioneer and perfecter' of this faith.
13052: Underlying reality or substance (the Son is the 'exact imprint of his hypostasis', Heb 1:3), also firm confidence. Faith gives present reality to what is hoped for.
13055: A leader who goes first and opens the way for others to follow, like a trailblazer or the founder of a city. Jesus leads 'many sons and daughters to glory' through suffering.
13058: One who runs ahead and enters first so others can follow; Jesus has gone 'behind the curtain' as forerunner, anchoring the hope of those who come after.
13061: Decisively and unrepeatably. Contrasts with the yearly Yom Kippur rite and the daily offerings; Christ's self-offering does not need repeating.
13064: God's own rest and the promised inheritance; sabbatismos (perhaps coined) suggests the festive Sabbath celebration of the world to come.
13067: Drawn from Exodus 25:40: what Moses built followed a heavenly pattern. A shadow is real and points to its source; the earthly sanctuary was a true, God-given sketch of the heavenly reality.
13070: In the Greek city, the free citizen's right to speak openly; here the right of access to God's presence and the courage to confess Jesus publicly despite shame.
13073: Public loss of honour in a society built on reputation. Hebrews treats sharing Christ's reproach as honour in God's court.
13076: A synagogue-style sermon that both encourages and urges. The same phrase is used for Paul's synagogue address in Acts 13:15.
